name: Émérillon
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gordon, Matthew & Françoise Rose. 2006. Émérillon stress: a phonetic and phonological study. Anthropological Linguistics 48(2): 132-168 (HAL author manuscript halshs-00453566, 43 pp; the HAL cover sheet gives pp. 125-143, Rose's own later reference lists give 132-168). Restated in Rose, Françoise. 2008. A typological overview of Emerillon, a Tupi-Guarani language from French Guiana. Linguistic Typology 12(3): 431-460, §2.3 p. 435 (HAL halshs-00724352).
catalog_locator: Gordon & Rose 2006, HAL ms halshs-00453566: §4 'Basic phonological generalizations', ms p. 6 for the rule; ms p. 7 for the optional initial clash stress; §4.1 ms pp. 8-10 and §4.2 ms p. 11 for the exceptions; abstract ms p. 1 and §6.1 ms pp. 20-21 for the phrase domain. Rose 2008 (HAL halshs-00724352): §2.3 'Stress', p. 435.
catalog_quote: Both impressionistic and acoustic analysis of the elicited data indicates that words are parsed into moraic trochees from right-to-left (Hayes 1995). With few exceptions, primary stress falls on a final heavy syllable (CVC, since Émérillon lacks CVV), otherwise on the penult, and secondary stress falls on alternating syllables counting backward from the primary stress. ... One complication arises in words with stress on the second syllable. Such words have an optional secondary stress on the initial syllable (depending on the speaker and the particular token), even though this creates a stress clash between the first two syllables. [§4, ms pp. 6-7] ... Results indicate that the domain of stress is the phrase with the metrical parse involving the formation of moraic trochees counting from the right edge of the phrase. [abstract] ... The domain of stress is the prosodic phrase. Primary stress (´) usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase. Secondary stress (`) alternates on every second syllable counting backward from the primary stress ... Optional stress can also be found on the initial syllable of the phrase. Besides, stress is attracted by heavy syllables, and is often avoided on high vowels in onsetless syllables. [Rose 2008: 435]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-to-left moraic trochees: primary stress on the final syllable if it is closed (CVC = heavy), otherwise on the penult; the count is computed over the prosodic phrase, so a word in isolation (= its own phrase) shows penult/final-heavy stress, but in connected speech a word's stress shifts with phrasal context.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second syllable counting leftward from the primary stress; an additional optional secondary stress on the phrase/word-initial syllable even when it clashes with a stressed second syllable (Gordon's 'binary plus clash' type); heavy CVC syllables attract stress and interrupt the count.
new_statements.exceptions: High vowels in onsetless open syllables reject stress (stress shifts left; such vowels often delete), giving variants like [ipoˈɨdʒ] ~ [iˌpoɨˈdʒ]; lexically stressed suffixes -pa (completive) and -tat (future) take final stress; a few irregular words (ãtɨ́ 'here', kɨtó 'frog' < Cariban loan, ideophone dɨ́rɨg, particle sinã́). In discourse, clash-initial stress is rarer and phrase-final syllables before a boundary tone can behave differently.
new_statements.domain_note: Authors state explicitly (abstract, §6.1) that the domain of stress is the prosodic phrase (often ≈ Intonation Unit), with moraic trochees built from the right edge of the phrase; the word-level rule quoted holds for citation forms because an isolated word constitutes a whole phrase. Rose 2008:435 repeats: 'The domain of stress is the prosodic phrase. Primary stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase.'
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Émérillon = Teko (emer1243) as a whole; Gordon & Rose 2006 data come from three speakers from western French Guiana (Camopi/Maroni area not dialectally distinguished) and one other speaker; no separate dialect glottocode applies.

sources.locator: Section 4 'Basic phonological generalizations', HAL author-manuscript p. 6 (halshs-00453566; published pp. 132-168); domain statement in section 6.1, ms pp. 20-21; restated in Rose 2008 Linguistic Typology 12: §2.3 p. 435 (file)
sources.note: Sec. 4: words parsed into moraic trochees right-to-left; primary stress on a final heavy (CVC) syllable, otherwise on the penult; secondary stress on alternating syllables counting back from the primary; optional initial secondary stress even under clash ('binary plus clash'); onsetless high vowels reject stress; sec. 4.2 a few lexically stressed suffixes (-pa, -tat) and irregular words; sec. 6.1: in discourse the domain of stress is the prosodic phrase (isolation word = phrase), so word-level patterns fluctuate with phrasal context; acoustic correlates duration/intensity, speaker-dependent.

sources.citation: Rose, Françoise. 2008. A typological overview of Emerillon, a Tupi-Guarani language from French Guiana. Linguistic Typology 12(3): 431-460. doi:10.1515/LITY.2008.044 (HAL halshs-00724352, publisher pagination)
sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Stress', p. 435: 'The domain of stress is the prosodic phrase. Primary stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase. Secondary stress alternates on every second syllable counting backward from the primary stress.. Optional stress can also be found on the initial syllable of the phrase. Besides, stress is attracted by heavy syllables, and is often avoided on high vowels in onsetless syllables.' Cites Gordon & Rose 2006.
